geodesic_distances — 3D geodesic op

• Data kinds: points → signal

• Call: import fullseye as fs; fs.ledger.geodesic_distances(points: numpy.ndarray, source: int, k: int = 8) -> numpy.ndarray (to call the implementation directly, import geodesic3d; geodesic3d.geodesic_distances(points: numpy.ndarray, source: int, k: int = 8) -> numpy.ndarray; from the registry, ops3d.get("geodesic_distances"))

Usage

Geodesic distances from a source to every point (Dijkstra on the kNN graph). → (N,) float (inf where unreachable).

Makes the k-nearest-neighbour graph built by knn_graph(points, k) (edge weight = Euclidean distance between points = chord length) undirected with directed=False, and solves single-source shortest paths with scipy.sparse.csgraph.dijkstra. d[i] is the path length on the graph from source to point i with d[source] = 0; points in connected components not connected to source are inf. Units are the coordinate units as-is.

• points: (N,3) point cloud (converted to float64).

• source: index of the start point (an integer in 0..N-1; out of range raises on the scipy side).

• k: number of neighbours (default 8). Too small splits the graph and increases inf; too large creates "shortcuts" that directly link distant surfaces, giving distances that do not follow the surface (both sides of a thin plate, folded-back surfaces, etc.).

Accuracy: edges are chord lengths, so arcs are slightly underestimated, while zigzag paths cause overestimation (see the bounding estimate by Bernstein et al. in the module docstring). If you have a triangle mesh, use geodesic_mesh, which does not depend on the number of neighbours. To subsample evenly by this distance, use farthest_point_sampling.
